title: Speaking practice: Trade Routes, Pill Bugs and Phone Plans
description: Eight speaking tasks: retell a story, explain a fence calculation, argue from an experiment, explain trade routes, present a science fair plan, summarize an article, justify a phone plan and present an animal fact card.

stimuli.title: Retell a story for a younger student
paragraphs: Your teacher asks you to retell a short story for a younger student who missed the lesson. Read the story summary below, then tell the story in your own words.

Story summary: Tomas lived in a village where the river flooded the fields every spring. Each year the villagers carried their grain up to the hills, but the work took many days. Tomas noticed that a row of old willow trees beside the field never washed away. One autumn he planted willow branches along the riverbank. His neighbors laughed at him. By the next spring the roots had grown deep, and the water moved slowly around the new trees instead of flooding the field. That year the villagers kept their grain at home, and many of them asked Tomas to teach them how to plant willows.

stimuli.title: Explain how to find the fence length
paragraphs: A rectangular garden bed is 9 meters long and 4 meters wide. The school wants to put a fence around the edge of the bed. The fence goes around all four sides, but there will be a gate 1 meter wide on one long side, and no fence is needed in the gate space. Your classmate was absent today and does not know how to find how much fence to buy.
Garden bed: 9 meters long, 4 meters wide. Gate: 1 meter wide, with no fence in that space.

stimuli.title: Where do pill bugs like to be?
paragraphs: Mei Lin did a science investigation and will share her results with the class. She made a box with two sides. One side had damp paper towel. The other side had dry paper towel. The temperature and the light were the same on both sides.
Trial 1: She put 10 pill bugs in the middle. After 5 minutes, 8 pill bugs were on the damp side and 2 were on the dry side.
Trial 2: She put 10 new pill bugs in the middle. After 5 minutes, 7 pill bugs were on the damp side and 3 were on the dry side.

stimuli.title: How trade routes changed places
paragraphs: Your class is studying long-distance trade routes in the ancient and medieval world. Your teacher gave you these notes and will ask you to explain them to the class.

Notes on the Silk Road: (1) The Silk Road was a network of land and sea routes. It linked China with places as far west as the Mediterranean Sea. (2) Traders carried goods such as silk, spices, and metal objects. (3) Traders also carried ideas, religions, and inventions. (4) Paper-making began in China and later spread to western Asia and Europe along trade routes. (5) Cities on the routes grew wealthy because traders needed markets, inns, and places to store goods.

stimuli.title: Tell a new classmate about Tuesday
paragraphs: Your school's science fair is on Friday. A family visitor named Ms. Rao asks what the day will be like. Here is the plan for the day:
9:00 Set up your project (gym)
9:40 Judges visit the projects (gym)
10:40 Break (hallway)
11:00 Open house for families (gym)
12:15 Lunch (cafeteria)
1:00 Awards (auditorium)
2:00 Clean up and go home (gym)

stimuli.title: Summarize an article about lending libraries
paragraphs: You read this short article and want to tell a friend about it. Your friend has not read it, so you need to summarize it in your own words.

In many neighborhoods, people can now borrow more than books. A “library of things” lends items such as ladders, sewing machines, camping tents, and baking pans. Members sign up for free or for a small fee and return the items after a week or two. Supporters say these libraries save money because few people need a ladder more than a few times a year. They also reduce waste, since fewer new products have to be made. Some libraries hold workshops where neighbors teach each other how to repair broken items. Critics point out that lending items takes volunteers and storage space, and that some tools wear out quickly. Even so, many towns have started their own.

stimuli.title: Choose a phone plan
paragraphs: The Okafor family is choosing between two phone plans. Plan A costs $20 each month plus $5 for each gigabyte of data used. Plan B costs $35 each month plus $2 for each gigabyte of data used.
Total cost for one month:
4 gigabytes: Plan A $40, Plan B $43
5 gigabytes: Plan A $45, Plan B $45
6 gigabytes: Plan A $50, Plan B $47
Mr. Okafor says: “Plan A is always cheaper, because its monthly fee is lower.”

stimuli.title: Fact card: the Arctic fox
paragraphs: A wildlife club is making a short audio guide for visitors. You will present facts about the Arctic fox from this fact card.
Arctic fox fact card
Home: the cold tundra in the far north.
Winter coat: thick white fur that keeps the fox warm and helps it blend in with snow.
Summer coat: brown or gray fur.
Ears: small and round. Small ears lose less body heat.
Feet: covered with fur, which keeps them warm on ice and snow.
Food: small animals, birds, and eggs.

items.stem: Retell the story of Tomas and the willow trees for a younger student. Tell the events in order and explain how the problem was solved.

checklist: I told what the problem was at the beginning.
I told the events in order, using words such as first, then, and after that.
I explained how Tomas solved the problem.
I told how the ending was different from the beginning.
exemplar: Names the problem (yearly floods and the hard work of moving grain) and the solution (willows planted along the bank).
Tells at least four events in a logical order with sequence words.
Uses past tense consistently and refers to the cause of the change (deep roots slowed the water).
Includes the neighbors' reaction and the ending, not only the middle.
Speaks clearly enough for a younger listener to follow.

support.clue: Think about the beginning (the problem), the middle (what Tomas did and how his neighbors reacted), and the end (what changed).
support.frame: In the beginning, ______ was a problem because ______. First, Tomas ______. Then, ______. After that, ______. In the end, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story): “In the beginning, Lena's school garden had no water because the pipe was broken. First, Lena asked the custodian for help. Then they collected rainwater in barrels. After that, the plants started to grow. In the end, the garden was green, and other classes copied her idea.” Now retell the story of Tomas the same way: the problem, the events in order, and the ending.

facts: Willow trees planted along a riverbank have roots that help hold soil in place.

items.stem: Explain to your classmate, step by step, how to find how much fence the school needs to buy. Say each step and tell the total.

checklist: I said what I need to find.
I used the numbers 9, 4, and 1 correctly.
I explained the steps in order, including what to do about the gate.
I said the total with the unit, meters.
exemplar: Identifies that the fence first goes around the whole rectangle (the perimeter) before the gate is considered.
Uses both given measurements and recognizes that there are two sides of each length.
Explains the steps in order with sequence words (first, then, finally) and says why the 1 meter gate space is taken away.
States the correct total of 25 meters with its unit.
Uses terms such as length, width, add, and subtract.

support.clue: Picture walking all the way around the garden. How many sides do you pass, and how long is each one? Then think about the gate.
support.frame: To find the fence length, I first find the distance around the whole bed. The garden is ___ meters long and ___ meters wide. First, I ______. Then, I ______ because ______. The school must buy ______ meters of fence.
support.model: Mentor example (a different shape): “To find the ribbon needed around a square card, I add all four sides. The card is 5 centimeters on each side. First, I write 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 and add the numbers to get 20. Then, I add 2 more centimeters because the ends of the ribbon overlap. The ribbon must be 22 centimeters.” Now explain the garden fence in the same way, using the length, the width, and the gate.

facts: The perimeter of a rectangle is the sum of its four sides: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 meters.
With a 1 meter gate space that needs no fence, the fence needed is 26 − 1 = 25 meters.

items.stem: Make a claim about what kind of place pill bugs choose, and support it with evidence from Mei Lin's two trials.

checklist: I stated a claim about what pill bugs choose.
I used numbers from both trials as evidence.
I used a word such as because or so to give a reason.
exemplar: States a clear claim (pill bugs prefer or choose damp places).
Cites specific counts from both trials (8 and 2; 7 and 3).
Connects the evidence to the claim with a linking word.
May note that the result happened twice, which makes it more trustworthy.
Speaks in complete sentences with scientific wording such as damp, dry, and trial.

support.clue: Look at the two numbers in each trial. Which side had more pill bugs each time?
support.frame: My claim is that pill bugs choose ______ places. In Trial 1, ___ pill bugs went to the ______ side and ___ went to the ______ side. In Trial 2, ______. This shows that ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different investigation): “My claim is that seeds sprout faster in warm places. In Cup 1, in the warm window, 6 of 10 seeds sprouted in four days. In Cup 2, in the cold closet, 1 of 10 seeds sprouted. This shows warm places help seeds sprout because more seeds sprouted in the warm window.” Now make your own claim about pill bugs and use the numbers.

facts: Pill bugs (woodlice) prefer damp places.
Trial 1: 8 + 2 = 10 pill bugs. Trial 2: 7 + 3 = 10 pill bugs.
Across both trials, 15 of 20 pill bugs were on the damp side.

items.stem: Explain to your class how trade routes like the Silk Road affected the places along them. Give at least two effects and connect each effect to its cause.

checklist: I named at least two effects of the trade routes.
I connected each effect to a cause.
I used words such as because, as a result, or therefore.
I used details from the notes.
exemplar: Identifies at least two effects (spread of ideas and inventions such as paper-making; growth of wealthy trading cities).
Links each effect to a specific cause from the notes (traders carried goods and ideas; traders needed markets and inns).
Uses cause-and-effect connectors accurately.
Uses academic vocabulary such as route, trade, goods, and spread.
Organizes the talk with an opening statement and a closing sentence.

support.clue: Notes 3 to 5 each show something that moved or grew because of trade. Ask: what moved, and what changed because of it?
support.frame: Trade routes like the Silk Road affected places along them in two ways. First, ______ because ______. As a result, ______. Second, ______ because ______. Therefore, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different topic): “The new highway affected the village in two ways. First, more trucks stopped to buy food because the highway passed nearby. As a result, the village cafes opened longer hours. Second, young people could travel to the city for school because the trip became shorter. Therefore, more of them finished high school.” Now explain what trade routes did to the places along them.

facts: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes linking China with the Mediterranean region.
Paper-making began in China and later spread westward along trade routes.
Cities along trade routes often grew wealthy from trade.

items.stem: Present the science fair plan to Ms. Rao in order. Give the time and the place for at least five parts of the day, and tell her which is longer, the judges' visit or the open house.

checklist: I told the plan in order.
I gave a time and a place for at least five parts of the day.
I said which is longer, the judges' visit or the open house, and gave a reason.
I used order words such as first, next, after that, and finally.
exemplar: Presents at least five items in the correct order with matching times and places.
Uses time expressions accurately (at 9:40, after the judges, before lunch).
Correctly identifies the open house (75 minutes) as longer than the judges' visit (60 minutes) and supports it with the times.
Uses transitions to organize the talk, with a brief opening and closing.
Speaks clearly with appropriate pace for a new listener.

support.clue: Read the times down the list. For each part, find when it starts and when the next part starts. Then subtract to find how long it lasts.
support.frame: First, at ______, you ______ in the ______. Next, at ______, ______. After that, ______. The ______ is longer because it lasts ___ minutes, but the ______ lasts ___ minutes.
support.model: Mentor example (a different schedule): “On Saturday, the swim club meets in order. First, at 9:00, you warm up in the shallow pool. Next, at 9:30, you practice kicking in Lane 2. After that, at 10:15, you take a rest on the benches. The rest lasts 15 minutes, but the warm-up lasts 30 minutes, so the warm-up is longer.” Now tell Dara about Tuesday in the same way.

facts: Judges' visit: 9:40 to 10:40 = 60 minutes.
Open house: 11:00 to 12:15 = 75 minutes.
The open house is 15 minutes longer than the judges' visit.

items.stem: Summarize the main idea of the article for a friend. Include two supporting details and one concern, and use your own words instead of reading the sentences exactly.

checklist: I stated the main idea in one or two sentences.
I gave two supporting details.
I mentioned one concern or criticism.
I used my own words and linking words such as however, because, and also.
exemplar: States an accurate main idea (libraries that lend everyday items benefit neighborhoods).
Includes two supporting details such as saving money, reducing waste, or repair workshops.
Includes a concern (needs volunteers and space, or tools wear out) and signals contrast with a word such as however.
Paraphrases rather than reading sentences word for word.
Organizes the summary clearly: main idea, details, concern, closing.

support.clue: Ask three questions: What is this article mostly about? What good things do supporters say? What problems do critics mention?
support.frame: The article is mainly about ______. One benefit is ______ because ______. Another benefit is ______. However, critics say that ______. Overall, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different article): “The article is mainly about rooftop gardens in cities. One benefit is that they keep buildings cooler because plants block the sun. Another benefit is that they give people a place to grow food. However, critics say that the roofs must be strong enough to hold the soil. Overall, rooftop gardens help cities if they are built carefully.” Now summarize the article about lending libraries in the same way.

facts: Tool and equipment lending libraries (“libraries of things”) exist in many communities and lend household items.

items.stem: Tell Mr. Okafor whether his statement is true. Use the costs listed to justify your answer, and recommend a plan for a family that uses 6 gigabytes in one sentence.

checklist: I said clearly whether Mr. Okafor is right or wrong.
I used the costs for 4, 5, and 6 gigabytes as evidence.
I compared the two plans with numbers.
I recommended a plan in one sentence and gave a reason.
exemplar: States that the claim is not always true.
Cites specific costs: Plan A is cheaper at 4 gigabytes ($40 and $43), the plans cost the same at 5 ($45), and Plan B is cheaper at 6 ($47 and $50).
Explains the reason the order changes (a lower fee but a higher price per gigabyte for Plan A).
Recommends Plan B for 6 gigabytes in one sentence and states the savings of $3.
Uses comparison language (cheaper, the same as, more expensive than, as the data increases).

support.clue: Compare the two prices on each line of the list. Look for the line where the cheaper plan changes.
support.frame: Mr. Okafor's statement is ______ because ______. At 4 gigabytes, Plan A costs ___ and Plan B costs ___, so ______. At 5 gigabytes, ______. At 6 gigabytes, ______. For a family that uses 6 gigabytes, I recommend Plan ___ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation): “Leo says Shop X is the best deal because it costs less for the first hour. This is not true. For 1 hour, Shop X costs $6 and Shop Y costs $7. For 2 hours, both cost $10. For 3 hours, Shop X costs $14 and Shop Y costs $13. For a three-hour ride, I recommend Shop Y because it is $1 cheaper.” Now answer Mr. Okafor with the phone plan costs.

facts: At 6 gigabytes, Plan B is $50 − $47 = $3 cheaper.

items.stem: Present the Arctic fox to the visitors. Describe three body features and tell how each one helps the fox live in a cold place.

checklist: I told where the Arctic fox lives.
I described three body features.
I told how each feature helps the fox.
I spoke in complete sentences.
exemplar: Identifies the habitat (cold tundra in the far north).
Describes at least three features accurately (thick fur, small ears, coat color change, furry feet).
Connects each feature to its purpose (stays warm, blends in, loses less heat).
Uses descriptive noun groups such as thick white fur and small round ears.
Speaks in a clear, organized way suitable for visitors.

support.clue: Most features on the card are followed by a reason. Look for words like keeps, helps, and loses less.
support.frame: The Arctic fox lives in ______. One body feature is its ______. This helps the fox ______. Another feature is ______. This helps because ______. A third feature is ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different animal): “The camel lives in the hot desert. One body feature is its wide, flat feet. These help the camel walk on soft sand without sinking. Another feature is its long eyelashes. They help keep sand out of its eyes. A third feature is its hump, which stores fat.” Now present the Arctic fox in the same way.

facts: Arctic foxes live in the cold tundra of the far north.
Their thick fur keeps them warm.
Their coat is white in winter and brown or gray in summer.
Small ears lose less body heat than large ears.
Their feet are covered with fur, which keeps them warm on ice and snow.
They eat small animals, birds, and eggs.
